verses.text: “Call now; is there any who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For resentment kills the foolish man, and jealousy kills the simple.
I have seen the foolish taking root, but suddenly I cursed his habitation.
His children are far from safety. They are crushed in the gate. Neither is there any to deliver them,
whose harvest the hungry eats up, and take it even out of the thorns. The snare gapes for their substance.
For affliction doesn’t come out of the dust, neither does trouble spring out of the ground;
but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.
“But as for me, I would seek God. I would commit my cause to God,
who does great things that can’t be fathomed, marvelous things without number;
who gives rain on the earth, and sends waters on the fields;
so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.
He frustrates the devices of the crafty, So that their hands can’t perform their enterprise.
He takes the wise in their own craftiness; the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong.
They meet with darkness in the day time, and grope at noonday as in the night.
But he saves from the sword of their mouth, even the needy from the hand of the mighty.
So the poor has hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.
“Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.
For he wounds, and binds up. He injures, and his hands make whole.
He will deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil shall touch you.
In famine he will redeem you from death; in war, from the power of the sword.
You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither shall you be afraid of destruction when it comes.
At destruction and famine you shall laugh, neither shall you be afraid of the animals of the earth.
For you shall be allied with the stones of the field. The animals of the field shall be at peace with you.
You shall know that your tent is in peace. You shall visit your fold, and shall miss nothing.
You shall know also that your offspring  shall be great, Your offspring as the grass of the earth.
You shall come to your grave in a full age, like a shock of grain comes in its season.
Look this, we have searched it, so it is. Hear it, and know it for your good.”

footnotes.content: Eliphaz pushes Job toward the hard truth: when we're caught in suffering, calling out to our friends won't ultimately save us. There's a loneliness to pain that other people's words cannot breach—until we turn to the Lord himself. The holy ones he mentions are God's own counsel, and that's where real help waits.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Resentment is a poison we drink hoping someone else will die—and jealousy works the same way. I've watched good people waste themselves in anger at the world, and their own spirits wither first. The Lord doesn't ask us to stay happy; He asks us to lay down the weight that bitterness carries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fool's roots look sturdy for a season, but Eliphaz saw what came next—sudden judgment, habitation cursed. I've noticed that people who build on dishonesty don't crumble gently. The Lord doesn't let such things sprawl unchecked forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When a parent builds on sand—pride, greed, cruelty—the children inherit the ruin. Eliphaz describes children crushed in the gate where justice is dispensed, abandoned because no deliverer comes. It's a hard saying, but it reflects a hard truth: our choices ripple into the next generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hungry harvest what the fool meant to keep; snares catch what remained. In ancient law, fields left unharvested belonged to the poor—here, the crooked man loses everything anyway. The Lord has a quiet way of distributing justice. Even the thorns yield what was meant to be stolen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Affliction doesn't just bubble up out of nothing, like vapors from the ground. There's always a reason—sometimes our own foolishness, sometimes the enemy's malice, sometimes the Lord's own wise pruning. Eliphaz wants Job to stop treating suffering as random chaos and start looking for its root.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is plain truth: trouble is as much a human inheritance as breath itself. We're born for it, like sparks fly upward from fire. It's not a curse, it's a condition—and that frees us from the bitter shock of asking 'why is this happening to me?' It's happening because we're alive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here Eliphaz turns a corner. 'But as for me'—he sets himself apart from the foolish and commits his whole case to God, like placing a sealed letter in the Lord's own hand. It's the pivot point of his counsel: don't defend yourself, don't rage, just hand it over to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's works are beyond our fathoming, His wonders past numbering—not because He hides from us, but because His mind is infinite and ours is not. Eliphaz reminds Job that the One he's about to seek is worthy of trust precisely because His wisdom exceeds our ability to track it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rain on the earth, waters on the fields—simple, daily gifts that sustain all life. The Lord whose works are beyond fathoming still remembers the dust, still sends what the growing things need. His greatness and His gentleness toward the small are one and the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The low are set on high; the mourning are exalted to safety. The Lord reverses the world's scorecards. What looks like loss to the world—meekness, sorrow—becomes the very condition through which He lifts us up. I've seen this reversed so many times I'd stake my life on it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The crafty make their plans with confidence, thinking themselves too clever for God to touch—and then their hands drop helpless. Eliphaz paints a picture of human pride meeting divine frustration, not in anger but in simple thwarting. Their strength becomes useless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wise catch themselves in their own trap. Their cunning, which they so carefully honed, becomes the very snare. I've watched clever people outwit themselves over and again. There's a sober wisdom in knowing that scheming against God is the only true foolishness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At midday they stumble through darkness, groping like blind men. The Lord doesn't always strike with lightning; sometimes He simply blinds the eyes of those who refused to see. They taste the very confusion and helplessness they meant for others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mouth of the wicked is like a sword, but the Lord saves the needy from it. I've seen frightened people rescued from oppressors—not always by might, but by the Lord's quiet intervention. He stands between the defenseless and those who would devour them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poor finds hope in this God, and injustice is rendered speechless—shamed into silence by His righteousness. Where the world sees only ruin, the Lord's justice opens a door. Injustice can't speak in the presence of His light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Happy is the one God corrects? It sounds like folly at first, but Eliphaz points to a deeper joy: being corrected by the Almighty is a sign of His love, not His enmity. The one He lets stumble and disciplines is the one He claims as His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He wounds and binds; He injures and heals. The same hands that strike are the hands that bind up the wound. There's no cruelty in God's correction—only the tenderness of a father who wounds to save. The binding comes with the wound.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six troubles, seven troubles—in the ancient pattern, this means all possible troubles, endless trials. The promise isn't that trouble won't come, but that through it all, evil won't touch the one the Lord is keeping. Numbers here mean 'however many, however long.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Famine is the slow death, war is the quick one—yet in both the Lord redeems. The word 'redeem' means He buys us back, snatches us from death's price. Whether we starve or fall by the sword, His rescue arm reaches into both.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The scourge of the tongue—slander, false words, the wounds words leave—and destruction when it comes. The Lord hides us from both. That's not meaning we'll never hear a harsh word, but that they won't have power to destroy what He protects.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To laugh at famine and destruction, to feel no fear of the beasts—this is the peace that comes from knowing you're held. It's not the laughter of denial but the freedom of a soul resting in God's hands. When you know He's got you, what's left to fear?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A covenant with the stones, peace with the field's beasts—the language echoes God's old promise to His people. Even creation itself becomes your covenant partner when you're at peace with God. The earth and its creatures recognize the one whom the Lord keeps.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your tent is in peace; when you visit your fold, nothing will be missing. Peace isn't the absence of activity—it's the security of coming home and finding all intact. It's the shepherd's confidence that the Lord has watched what matters most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your offspring will be great, as numerous and vigorous as grass—the future is open and flourishing. This promise speaks to permanence, to the hope that what you've built will endure and grow. It's the Lord's way of saying your life has meant something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To come to your grave in a full age, like grain gathered in its season—the image is of a life completed, harvested in God's time, not cut off too soon. It's the promise of a natural end, ripeness, the sense of having reached what was meant. Not every life gets that grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliphaz closes with 'we have searched it, so it is'—these aren't new words, but tested truth passed down through generations who've walked hard roads and come out the other side knowing God. Readers today hear an echo of that ancient confidence: the Lord's faithfulness is not theory; it's the worn wisdom of every faithful heart across the centuries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
